extracted.intended_audience: students and educated readers of natural philosophy / evolutionary theory
extracted.subtask_description: A chapter-length exposition distinguishing 'simple' and 'compound' evolution: it states a general physical law (evolution as integration of matter and dissipation of motion) and derives conditions (rate of redistribution, contained motion, material state, composition, water/heat content) under which evolution is simple or becomes compound, with physical, chemical, and biological examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evolution as integration of matter and dissipation of motion
rubrics_metrics.description: Evolution is fundamentally an integration of Matter and dissipation of Motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the central principle to be kept in view: the 'total history of every sensible existence is included in its Evolution and Dissolution'. All subsequent distinctions (simple vs compound) are framed with reference to this definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple vs compound evolution determined by rate of primary redistribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Primary re-distribution ends in forming aggregates which are simple where it is rapid, but which become compound in proportion as its slowness allows the effects of secondary re-distributions to accumulate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rapid integration (e.g., sudden crystallization or deposition from solution) yields simple evolution with no appreciable secondary rearrangements; slow, gradual concentration (e.g., slow cooling/condensation) permits secondary motions/currents and thus compound evolution. Example: sal-ammoniac vapor condensing suddenly into crystals (simple) vs gradual condensation producing currents and extensive secondary rearrangement (compound).

rubrics_metrics.name: Contained motion quantity governs ease of secondary redistribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Incident forces work secondary re-distributions easily when the contained motion is large in quantity; they work them with increasing difficulty as the contained motion diminishes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanical agitation, molecular vibration (heat), or forms that include significant internal motion (liquids, gases, colloids) allow incident forces to produce secondary rearrangements. Examples: shaking a vessel of fragments; annealing steel; heating chemical mixtures to cause reactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permanence of secondary redistribution requires low contained motion
rubrics_metrics.description: Large amounts of secondary re-distribution are possible only where there is a great quantity of contained motion, and these re-distributions can have permanence only where the contained motion has become small.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This highlights a tension: conditions favoring abundant secondary change (high motion) oppose those favoring permanence (low motion). Permanent structural changes arise when a system can undergo secondary rearrangements while later becoming sufficiently rigid/solid to fix those changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heat/ agitation facilitates molecular rearrangement and chemical change
rubrics_metrics.description: Adding to molecular motion (heat) or mechanical agitation increases the facility with which constituents re-arrange; chemical unions and disunions are aided by rise of temperature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations: shaking fragments in a vessel causes settling and segregation by density; temperature rise increases rates of precipitation and chemical reaction; tempering steel/annealing glass allow internal redistribution by raising molecular agitation. Anti-pattern: assuming reactions or rearrangements proceed without sufficient agitation/heat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sudden solidification (crystallization) suppresses secondary redistributions
rubrics_metrics.description: When molecular motion is dissipated suddenly and integration is abrupt (crystallization or sudden solidification), the process is essentially simple: little or no appreciable secondary re-distributions accompany the primary change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: vapor forming crystals on a cold surface; crystals deposited from solution by sudden loss of molecular motion. Contrast with gradual condensation where secondary currents produce additional local rearrangements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liquid/plastic states permit more internal redistribution than solid states
rubrics_metrics.description: Liquid form implies a greater quantity of contained motion than solid form; plastic (liquid-solid) aggregates permit internal redistribution with comparative facility and persistence until further solidification fixes the arrangement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: magmas ground with water allow heavier components to settle while thin; as water evaporates and mixture thickens, segregation is impeded. Plastic state permits re-distributions that become persistent as the body solidifies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complexity and gaseous-derived components increase molecular heat and instability
rubrics_metrics.description: In general, the molecular heat of a compound increases with degree of complexity; compounds formed from elements that ordinarily contain much motion (gaseous elements) have combinations less stable and are more readily decomposed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: complex molecules or those containing gaseous elements are more liable to decomposition/re-distribution when molecular motion is increased. Example: nitrogenous compounds absorb heat on formation and are especially unstable—explosive substances are nitrogenous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chemical composition correlates with structural change capacity (organic vs inorganic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Organic aggregates combine large quantities of contained motion with concentration/cohesion, enabling extensive secondary redistributions; their chemical constitution (nitrogenous, colloid form, proteins with gaseous components, high water content) accounts for this peculiarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Details: proteins contain gaseous elements and thus lock large motion into small space; organic molecules form colloid (clusters of clusters) rather than crystalloid arrangements; water provides molecular mobility and plasticity. These traits reconcile high contained motion with persistent structure in organisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amount of water correlates with degree and rate of secondary redistribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Other things equal, there is a direct relation between the amount of re-distribution and the amount of contained water: greater water content -> greater structural modifiability and faster change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence: cutting off water supply arrests formative changes in plants; desiccation can render certain lower animals torpid but revivable on rehydration; young tissues with higher water ratios change faster than older/drier tissues; shoots and tips change faster than trunks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temperature (heat) correlates with rates of structural change across organisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Amounts of structure and rates of structural change generally increase with temperature: organisms/tissues at higher temperatures show greater activity and complexity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and contrasts: animals typically have higher 'heat' and more rapid structural change than plants; vertebrates are warmer/higher activity than invertebrates; mammals and birds exhibit higher molecular agitation and greater multiformity than fishes or reptiles. Plant growth resumes in warm greenhouses despite lower light—temperature is limiting.

rubrics_metrics.name: During gradual condensation secondary motions (currents) may dominate primary motion
rubrics_metrics.description: When a gaseous mass loses heat gradually and passes through liquid stage, molecular mobility permits easy re-arrangement and gives rise to secondary motions/currents which can be so important as to subordinate the primary integrating motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This explains why slow processes produce complex internal rearrangements: while volume contracts progressively, local currents and other motions effect substantial local re-distributions (e.g., currents during slow condensation). These motions are less visible after full solidification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plastic state enables persistent but changeable structures until further solidification
rubrics_metrics.description: A plastic state (semi-solid) allows re-distributions to occur though less readily than in liquids; such changes have a certain persistence and can become decided when further solidification fixes them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical consequence: structures formed in plastic states (e.g., certain ceramic pastes, currant-jelly crystallization on standing) can exhibit persistent heterogeneities if allowed to set; Mr. Babbage's porcelain paste example shows separation over time in a plastic state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correlated examples across scales support the generalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Phenomena at macroscopic/mechanical, molecular/chemical, and biological scales follow the same general law: greater contained motion permits easier redistribution; loss of motion tends toward integration and stability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text marshals examples from shaken vessels, tempering/annealing, precipitation from solutions, chemical decomposition with heat, and biological growth/aging to show the universality of the principle. Use cross-scale analogies when applying the law.
